newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwanda arrests 500 genocide suspects, says U.N..
newsitem.headline: Rwanda arrests 500 genocide suspects, says U.N..

text.p: Rwandan authorities have arrested at least 500 Hutu refugees accused of genocide among 340,000 to return from Tanzania this month, U.N. officials said on Monday.

U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) official Anne Willem Bijleveld told Reuters the refugees were arrested in Murambi commune in northeastern Rwanda in connection with the 1994 genocide of about 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
A Hutu refugee lobby group, the Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy to Rwanda (RDR), denounced on Monday what it called false allegations.
It said the returnees were being arrested on the basis of testimony by people who pretended to be former neighbours of the accused but wanted to keep houses and property they had stolen.

UNHCR spokesman Paul Stromberg in the Rwandan capital Kigali said: "Our understanding is that this is preventive detention as people gather around the trucks as the returnees disembark and indicate who they accuse of participating in the genocide."
"It seems they (authorities) don't have a lot of options other than protective detention to avoid vigilante violence. Obviously we hope their cases will be examined as quickly as possible," he added.
The RDR rejected the argument that the arrests were preventive detention.

The human rights group Amnesty International has accused UNHCR of violating its mandate by cooperating with what amounts to the expulsion of refugees after Tanzania set a December 31 deadline for all 540,000 Rwandan refugees to return home.
UNHCR said last Friday it was concerned at reports returnees from Tanzania were being arrested at Murambi and Nyagatare based on neighbours' suspicions of their role in the 1994 genocide.
UNHCR raised the arrests with Rwanda's justice minister and stressed that Rwandan law stipulated that any arrests should only be carried out in accordance with proper legal procedures.
The first genocide trials in Rwanda are scheduled to start on December 30 with two suspects accused of genocide and crimes against humanity, which carry a maximum sentence of death.
Tanzanian police and troops have been rounding up suspected members of Rwanda's former Hutu army and Interhamwe militiamen who led the genocide and therefore refuse to return.
Bijleveld said the Murambi arrests followed the slaughter of 15,000 people, or half the village's population, during the 1994 genocide.
"This was a village which had 30,000 inhabitants of which 15,000 were killed. Lots of people going back (to Rwanda from Tanzania) had to have a hand in it," the UNHCR official said.
Stromberg said more than 15,000 refugees entered Rwanda at the Rusumo crossing in northwestern Tanzania on Monday morning, taking the total to return so far in December to 340,000.
"We're now getting close to the tail end," said Bijleveld, adding the largest remaining column consisted of about 100,000 refugees and was 60 km (37 miles) from the border with Rwanda.
More than 600,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees returned home from eastern Zaire after fighting forced them out of their camps but hundreds of thousands have trekked deep into Zaire since last month.
